military.label: Military history
military.date_label: Earlier roots · Howard 1961 · Keegan 1976 · multiple paradigms
military.description: Studies campaigns and combat alongside institutions, societies, maritime power, gender and remembrance. Ancient historians such as Thucydides and Polybius already wrote about testing reports of battle, terrain and military experience; they are precursors of the genre, not its founders. From about 1900 the field was practised in archive-based campaign and army histories, university lectureships and chairs (Oxford 1905 and 1909), official histories of the world wars and an American society (1933) and journal (1937; renamed Military Affairs in 1941); much of this work was written by or for officers. Howard’s contextual reconstruction, Keegan’s critical study of battle and debates over military revolutions supply different methods and explanations. Source access, narrative framing and geographic scope shape their claims.
military.representative_figures_and_works: Ancient precursors include Thucydides and Polybius on testing reports, terrain and experience; modern roots include Clausewitz, On War (1832), and Hans Delbrück; from c. 1900, Charles Oman and J. W. Fortescue wrote archive-based campaign and army history, Grundy and Kromayer surveyed ancient battlefields, and general-staff and cabinet historical sections wrote official histories of the world wars (Edmonds from 1922; the US Army’s World War II series, such as Matloff and Snell, 1953); later examples: Michael Howard, John Keegan, and Joanna Bourke.

military.scope_note: A research field with overlapping objects, not one school or a progression that supersedes campaign history. Delbrück, campaign and army historians, official historians and strategic writers supply distinct resources; military historians also reinterpret and criticize them. Keegan’s restricted battle definition leaves much colonial and guerrilla experience outside its frame. European military-revolution debates extend to overseas encounters without representing the whole world’s military historiography. Bourke, Winter and Nell retain distinct questions about bodies, mourning and recognition. Scholarly collaboration, library work, editing and archival limits are part of the field’s production. Ancient writers who narrated and judged wars (Thucydides, Polybius, Arrian) are selected precursors. The selected ancient passages document statements about testimony, terrain and experience. Separately checked modern passages discuss these authors; Kromayer explicitly engages Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. These examples do not establish continuous transmission. Clausewitz ranked ancient military history the least useful while allowing instructive exceptions. Official and semi-official histories were written from privileged records, read in proof by participants or framed by sponsoring institutions; Liddell Hart criticised them in the period. Karsten (1984), describing the ‘new’ military history, concedes that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. The selection before 1960 concentrates on British, American and German scholarship; other historiographies of war are not surveyed here.

strands.title: War studies, research and teaching
strands.focus: Howard became lecturer in military studies at King’s in 1953; a new War Studies programme was approved in 1955. His King’s work combines historical study with wider social, ethical and political inquiry. Earlier work and institutional support included Laughton’s naval history, Maurice’s chair of military studies (1927; the department closed in 1948), and C. K. Webster and Hancock, whose official-history work had drawn them to war as a field. Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022) call the story of Howard rescuing the subject from an academic wilderness one he ‘consciously cultivated’. Library access, publishing and translation collaboration form part of the research setting.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); War in European History (1976)

strands.title: Official and semi-official history and its critics
strands.focus: General-staff and cabinet historical sections wrote large histories of the world wars from privileged records. Edmonds’s British volumes (from 1922) were ‘based on the British official records’, written partly for ‘students at military schools’ and read in proof by officers who took part. Morison’s naval history was commissioned with full records access yet declared ‘in no sense an official history’ (1947). In the US Army’s series, Matloff and Snell, formerly instructors in history and English respectively and both wartime servicemen, joined the project in 1946; their volume’s foreword, by the Chief of Military History, asked readers to see its controversies as differences ‘among comrades in arms’ (1953), and its preface credits Helen McShane Bailey’s knowledge of the War Department’s records and Evelyn Cooper’s statistics. Liddell Hart attacked documentary and ‘camouflaged’ history (1930, 1944). During and after the Second World War official commissions drew academic historians to war (Hancock and Gowing from 1941, Webster and Frankland from 1950, Howard from 1959), under closure rules and secrecy. Later studies of the genre are unread here, and the German and French official histories are known only from period mentions.

(1944); Morison, Operations in North African Waters (1947), foreword and introduction; Matloff and Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953), foreword and preface; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Howard, Grand Strategy, vol. strands.title: Campaign and army history as scholarship, c. 1898–1950
strands.focus: Oman’s art-of-war volume (1898) and Peninsular War (1902) worked from chronicles, Record Office papers and passages omitted from printed dispatches, treated veterans’ memoirs with caution and walked battlefields. Fortescue, a civilian, wrote the army’s history as political as well as military history (1899) and distrusted regimental histories; his 1914 definition held that ‘below a certain stage of civilisation, there can be no military history’, a boundary that bears on the field’s geographic scope. Parker’s preface (1928) proposes an institutional history of the Roman legions’ organisation, recruitment and service; the abbreviation list shows extensive inscription corpora, and the body is unread. Kromayer and Veith’s preface (1928) adds strategy and tactics to the antiquarian study of ancient armies and excludes the Orient, Carthage, Gauls and Germans. Howard (1961, as reported by Kitchen and Mitchell and by Strachan) later named regimental ‘nursery history’ and the historian’s duty to examine its ‘myth’.
strands.works: Oman, A History of the Art of War: The Middle Ages (1898) and A History of the Peninsular War, vol. I (1902), prefaces; Fortescue, A History of the British Army, vols. I–II (1899), preface, and Military History (1914); Parker, The Roman Legions (1928); Kromayer and Veith, Heerwesen und Kriegführung der Griechen und Römer (1928); Howard, ‘The Use and Abuse of Military History’ (1961 lecture; 1962)

strands.title: Chairs, journals and the soldier-scholar before 1960
strands.focus: In the British institutions examined here, university teaching developed alongside officer education. Oxford made military history a special subject after the South African War, created a lectureship in 1905 and a chair in 1909, whose first holder, Spenser Wilkinson, called military history ‘the effort to understand war’; the chair, vacant from 1939, went to Cyril Falls in 1946 rather than Liddell Hart. Trinity College, Cambridge, appointed Fortescue its first lecturer in military history in 1913. At King’s College London Frederick Maurice held a chair of military studies from 1927; the department closed in 1948. In the United States the American Military History Foundation was incorporated in 1933 after discussions among ‘military and civilian archival personnel’; its journal (1937) became Military Affairs in 1941 and nearly collapsed in 1957. Strachan (2002) calls Liddell Hart and Falls ‘in many ways more a journalist than an academic’ and writes that before Howard’s appointment almost nobody who studied the history of war had not experienced it.
strands.works: Wilkinson, The University and the Study of War (1909); Fortescue, Military History (1914), lecture I; Maurice, ‘On the Uses of the Study of War’ (1927), as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch; Society for Military History chronology (1933–69 entries)

strands.title: War, state and society before the ‘new military history’
strands.focus: Wilkinson’s inaugural lecture (1909) held that ‘as the State is, so will its army be’ and that in war ‘the architectonic art is policy or politics, not strategy or generalship’. Maurice (1927, as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch) counted statecraft, economics, raw materials, science, industry and civilian morale as of ‘prime importance’ to the study of war. Hancock, editing the civil official histories, treated the armed forces as ‘no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’ (as quoted by the same authors). Roberts (1955) proposed tactical change with wider institutional effects. Quincy Wright’s foreword (1942) describes a study of war begun at the University of Chicago in 1926 that involved ‘over fifty studies by research assistants and members of the faculty’; only the foreword is read. Karsten (1984) calls such questions the ‘new’ military history while conceding that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. Hintze, Vagts, Ritter and Ropp are not yet read for this entry.
strands.works: Wilkinson (1909); Maurice, inaugural lecture (1927); Wright, A Study of War (1942), foreword; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Roberts, ‘The Military Revolution, 1560–1660’ (1955 lecture); Karsten (1984), opening

strands.title: Ancient historians on testimony, terrain and experience
strands.focus: Thucydides tests eyewitness accounts against one another and says Spartan secrecy and bragging prevent accurate numbers at Mantinea. Polybius requires the study of documents, the survey of places and political experience, holds that no one without experience of war can write well about it, and judges Ephorus’ land battles by the ground; his polemic is also self-promotion. Arrian prefers Ptolemy and Aristobulus because they served on the campaign. Grundy (1911) calls Thucydides’ narrative ‘in the main a military history’ subordinated to political teaching, and Kromayer (1903) adopts and qualifies Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. Delbrück (1913, p. 16) asks: ‘Ought we to believe what Caesar informs us of concerning the gigantic armies of the Gauls, whose conquest is his glory, since we have now seen that neither Napoleon nor Frederick in this respect is to be trusted?’; Caesar’s text itself was not read. Herodotus and Xenophon appear only through modern critics: Delbrück (1913) notes that Herodotus wrote ‘forty or fifty years after the events’, Grundy (1901) that in military matters he ‘seems to have possessed little, if any, special knowledge’, and Kromayer (1903, p. 93) finds Xenophon’s account of Mantinea one-sided. These writers are precursors of a genre, not a single origin of the field.
strands.works: Thucydides, History 1.22, 5.68; Polybius, Histories 12.25e–28a, 3.33, 3.48; Arrian, Anabasis, preface; Grundy (1901), preface, and (1911), pp. 7–9; Kromayer (1903), pp. 93–96; Delbrück, Numbers in History (1913), pp. 8–10, 16

events.label: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War (1.22, 5.68)
events.support: Placed only in the fifth century BCE: a contemporary narrator of the war who says he relied on what he saw and on tested reports (1.22) and recounts the battle of Mantinea, 418 BCE (5.68). The passages read do not date the composition, which may have continued after 401 BCE; ‘approximate’ marks that. A precursor of the genre, not the field’s beginning.

events.label: Polybius, Histories (12.25e–28a; 3.33, 3.48)
events.support: Placed only in the second century BCE: he consulted Hannibal’s own bronze tablet and questioned men present at the Alpine crossing (3.33, 3.48), writing in the generation after Hannibal’s war. No composition year is established by the passages read. A precursor, not a lineage.

events.label: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, preface

continuation.basis: The field is older and broader than these selected works; ancient precursors are not its beginning, and no researched universal interval is proposed.

chronology.interpretation: Use dated works with an explicit selective scope. Thucydides, Polybius and Arrian are context: precursors of the genre, placed only by century, not a lineage or the field’s first years. Oman, Fortescue, Delbrück, Grundy and Kromayer (1898–1903) are a selected cluster of modern scholarly work, not a foundation date; Kromayer’s 1900 expedition is context for his 1903 volume. Official and semi-official histories (Edmonds 1922, Morison 1947, Matloff and Snell 1953) and the American society and journal (1933, 1937) are selected later events, not the beginnings of official or American military history. Howard 1961 and Keegan 1976 are contributions to an older field, not its first and last years. Later memoir dates are evidence dates, not new personal interventions by Howard.
retain: Multiple paradigms, colonial/guerrilla limits of Keegan's frame, and collaboration/editorial labour.
Ancient precursors are not a continuous lineage; the modern selection concentrates on British, American and German scholarship.
unresolved: If phase bars are useful, define their subject and geography; do not construct a universal beginning from the oldest source in this selection.
Composition dates of the ancient works were not checked; they are placed by century only. Caesar, Herodotus and Xenophon are discussed only through modern critics and are not dated here.

political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.

social.label: New social history
social.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.

Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996). strands.title: Politics within social-history debate
strands.focus: Eley and Nield asked in 1980 why social history ignored politics (article unread; they recalled in 2007 that it 'drew disappointingly little response in print' and that they had been 'trying to create a space for political analysis in the expanded sense given to "politics" by the politics of knowledge of 1968', 2000, p. 14). Joyce's 'The End of Social History?' (1995; unread) drew their 'Starting Over' (1995; unread), which Joyce said equated his questioning of social history 'with contemporary neo-liberalism' (1996). In 'Farewell to the Working Class?' (2000, read in full) they held that 'class discursively understood … is a better starting point' while wanting 'to break this logic of disavowal' (p. 16); Scott's reply (read in full) called this 'Assent to Discourse' and objected that insisting on class forecloses other political categories (p. 69); Cooper answered that 'they did not think to ask Karl Marx' (p. 61). The debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980), coauthored; “Starting Over” (1995); “Farewell to the Working Class?” and reply (ILWCH 57, 2000); The Future of Class in History (2007)

memory.scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. Jelin’s Argentina project adds a pre-2000 case beyond Europe; it does not represent all Latin American memory work.

indigenous.scope_note: A selective grouping of independently rooted Indigenous historical practices and decolonizing research, with Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Māori, Osage, Native Hawaiian, Yukon and Australian examples. Earlier writing, community knowledge, academic historical scholarship and decolonizing methodology have different histories. Community historians, academic historians and outside collaborators have different positions. Neither anthropology nor European theory is their common origin; no selection stands for every nation or protocol. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. Academic Indigenous history includes documented collaborations with scholars working across historical, anthropological and geographical inquiries. Shared research subjects do not establish intellectual descent. Later source dates are separate from earlier events; only Leddy’s 2010 article is accepted here as a selected post-2000 intervention.

philhistory.label: Explanation & objectivity debates
philhistory.date_label: Earlier roots · Becker address 1931 · Hempel 1942 · Carr 1961 · Elton 1967
philhistory.description: Disputes concern general laws, understanding actions, historical facts, and the possibility of objectivity. Analytic philosophy’s covering-law debate overlaps with historians’ arguments about evidence and interpretation without being identical to them. Narrative theory enters a discussion already under way.

representative_people.context: Challenges reducing all historical explanations to a covering-law model; rational action and pragmatic questions are distinct concerns.
representative_people.works: Laws and Explanation in History (1957)

representative_people.works: What Is History? (1961)

settler_colonialism.label: Settler colonialism
settler_colonialism.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999, 2006 · journal 2011 · Tuck and Yang 2012 · critiques 2013–14 · TRC 2015 · Wolfe d. 2016 · Englert 2020 · reviewed through 2024
settler_colonialism.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, took land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe gave the field its programme: settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'invasion is a structure not an event' (1999, 2006). Lorenzo Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011) and distinguished colonialism ('you, work for me') from settler colonialism ('you, go away'), adding that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': it 'extinguishes itself'. Two questions organise this selection: how elimination persists while pursuing its own completion, and how settler-colonial analysis relates to Indigenous sovereignty, refusal and resurgence. Veracini develops Wolfe's formula: self-supersession means the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, not a successful decolonisation. The Indigenous reading adopts Wolfe's formula while insisting that 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies' (Kauanui), that 'decolonization is not a metaphor' (Tuck and Yang) and that refusal, not recognition, answers the settler state (Simpson, Coulthard). Settler scholars warn against 'colonial fatalism' (Macoun and Strakosch); Marxists ask whether elimination or exploitation defines the form (Englert). In Canada the frame met an older historiography of reserves, treaties, gender and the state, and the TRC's finding of 'cultural genocide' (2015).

settler_colonialism.scope_note: A research field whose consolidation came after 2000; reviewed through 2024 in the period-4 wave (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md). Read in full: Wolfe 2006 (in an Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page), Veracini 2011 and his 2016 obituary of Wolfe, Kauanui 2016, Englert 2020, Goeman 2016; in most pages, Tuck and Yang 2012 and Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014; Macoun and Strakosch 2013 in the authors' version; Veracini 2013 in its author manuscript (abstract, opening, conclusion); the TRC summary pp. 1–3. Unread, known through publisher pages or named readers: Wolfe 1999 beyond pp. 1–2, 2001, 2008, 2016; Veracini 2010, 2015; Coulthard; A. Simpson (book; 2017 abstract read); Byrd; Moreton-Robinson; L. B. Simpson; Rowse; Konishi; Sexton; Garba and Sorentino; King; Daschuk; Miller 2009; Perry 2015; Carter 2016; McCallum; Mawani; Stanger-Ross; Lowman and Barker; Regan. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies; Veracini (2013) and Kauanui (2016) both record uses of the term before Wolfe (Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973, Denoon 1983, Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis 1995). Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris, Miller, Daschuk and McCallum wrote earlier or beside it, and their publisher descriptions do not use the phrase. Critics appear as critics; Kauanui and Goeman defend Wolfe's theory against shallow citation while asking the field to attend to Indigenous studies. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: two or more of the field's authors are cited by 3.2% of Canada + US theses in 2000–09 and 11.0% in 2020–25 (Canada 15.2%, US 6.8%); Wolfe and Veracini are co-cited by 3.0% of theses in 2020–25 and Wolfe with Tuck and Yang, Simpson or Coulthard by 2.3% (the release's category 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' names a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position: Tuck and Yang build on Wolfe, and Kauanui criticises his reception), the only rising two-sided citing after 2000; the Canadian neighbourhood of the founders is the largest and youngest of any field (51 works, median year 2006), its 2020–25 entrants Coulthard, Simpson, Carter, Miller, Daschuk, Kauanui and Greer. The earlier pilot of 2026-10-12 (Canadian strict History PhDs, 2009–26) found 54 citing a work of Wolfe's and 17 the 1999 book (first in 2012), and Daschuk the work most co-cited with Wolfe and Veracini (19 of 58); these figures say more about Canadian history than about him. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Francophone uptake in the corpus remains near zero.

strands.title: Structure, not event: the logic of elimination
strands.focus: Wolfe's programme, now read in his own pages. Settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it 'is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'the primary motive for elimination is not race … but access to territory. Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event'; elimination has a 'positive' aspect (allotment, citizenship, child abduction, assimilation) that persists after the frontier, so that the form is 'relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' names its convergence with genocide without 'hierarchy among victims' (2006). The formula goes back to the 1999 book (p. 2) and the 1994 essay (p. 96, per his note 7). Kauanui: the phrase 'often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement of his theory'.

strands.title: Veracini: the field, the journal and the self-superseding structure
strands.focus: Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011; open access, volunteer-run, on an ARC grant; to Taylor & Francis in 2013) 'to contribute to the consolidation of a new scholarly field'. Colonialism says 'you, work for me'; settler colonialism says 'you, go away'; the two 'should be understood in their dialectical relation'. Developing Wolfe's formula rather than disputing it, he adds that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': 'settler colonialism, by contrast, extinguishes itself' and is 'least visible in the settler cities'. This self-supersession is the settler project's attempted extinction of the settler–Indigenous relation by the disappearance of Indigenous peoples, not a successful decolonisation, which would instead end 'with an indigenous ultimate permanence'; 'decolonisation is not settler decolonisation', and the politics of recognition 'cannot be considered a genuinely decolonising move' (2011). His history of the concept (2013) finds three earlier careers of the term and a consolidation 'from approximately the mid 1990s', with 'both the Canadian and US historiographies … late in adopting' it. Englert calls him Wolfe's 'self-styled intellectual successor'; Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel find in his history 'Indigenous studies and Indigenous resistance … pretty much erased'.

strands.title: The Indigenous reading: land, refusal, incommensurability
strands.focus: Indigenous political theory that takes up Wolfe's formula and redirects the field. Tuck and Yang: settler colonialism's violence 'is not temporally contained in the arrival of the settler but is reasserted each day of occupation. This is why Patrick Wolfe (1999) emphasizes that settler colonialism is a structure and not an event'; 'decolonization brings about the repatriation of Indigenous land and life; it is not a metaphor'; the settler–native–slave triad; 'settler moves to innocence'; 'an ethic of incommensurability' against reconciliation, which 'is about rescuing settler normalcy' (2012). Simpson: 'refusal' as 'an alternative to recognition politics in settler colonial society', consent 'as a technique of recognition and simultaneous dispossession' (2017, abstract; the 2014 book is known through its publisher page). Coulthard: settler colonialism 'territorially acquisitive in perpetuity'; in Canada the means of elimination changed but 'the ends have always remained the same: to shore up continued access to Indigenous peoples' territories' (2014, p. 125, as quoted by Englert); a 'place-based' reworking of primitive accumulation (publisher). Byrd and L. B. Simpson are unread and known only through catalogue metadata and other authors' citations; Moreton-Robinson is known through her publisher's checked description ('a white possession', 'the disavowal of Indigenous sovereignty'). These works have their own genealogies; in Canadian and US theses they are read with Wolfe (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23), and the user ruled (2026-10-12) that they may sit in more than one field.

Rowse: a 'teleology of elimination' (2014, abstract). Greer: one mode among several, dominant in some periods and regions (2019). Shoemaker: universal theory or English heritage? (2019). Englert: 'the elimination of the native … does not accurately define the overall logic of settler colonialism'; settler colonies in Africa and South America 'were built on the exploitation of indigenous peoples'; accumulation by dispossession 'carried out by all classes of settlers, including by workers' (2020, with Kelley and Speed 2017).

William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 369–374.; Jeffrey Ostler and Nancy Shoemaker, "Settler Colonialism in Early American History: Introduction," William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 361–368.

strands.title: Indigenous studies and the field: who made it, whom it displaces
strands.focus: Kauanui: Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did', yet 'he tends to be most frequently cited as if he had'; 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies'; indigeneity is 'a category of analysis that is distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality'; Warrior counted ASA panels and feared the field had become 'an answer to the chronic need for more attention to … Native and Indigenous studies' (2016). Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel: the field 'can displace, overshadow, or even mask over Indigenous studies'; 'when settlers take up these questions, it's suddenly considered a legitimate field of study' (2014). Goeman answers from the same field: Wolfe 'critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner' and his work 'became a place to engage Indigenous studies concerns in relation to settler colonial studies' (2016). Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge the field (2019, abstract).
strands.works: Shino Konishi, "First Nations Scholars, Settler Colonial Studies, and Indigenous History," Australian Historical Studies 50, no. 3 (2019): 285–304.; J. Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).; Corey Snelgrove, Rita Kaur Dhamoon and Jeff Corntassel, "Unsettling Settler Colonialism: The Discourse and Politics of Settlers, and Solidarity with Indigenous Nations," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 3, no. 2 (2014): 1–32.

strands.title: Slavery and Black studies critiques
strands.focus: How settler-colonial and decolonial frameworks place slavery and Black people. Wolfe 2006 (read) sets out the opposed racialisations of Black and Indigenous people in the United States; Tuck and Yang's settler–native–slave triad (read) is what Garba and Sorentino answer. Both authors' words are now read; the critics' remain at abstract level.
strands.works: Tapji Garba and Sara-Maria Sorentino, "Slavery Is a Metaphor: A Critical Commentary on Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang's 'Decolonization Is Not a Metaphor'," Antipode 52, no. 3 (2020): 764–782.; Jared Sexton, "The Vel of Slavery: Tracking the Figure of the Unsovereign," Critical Sociology 42, nos. 4–5 (2016): 583–597.; Tiffany Lethabo King, The Black Shoals: Offshore Formations of Black and Native Studies (Durham: Duke University Press, 2019).

strands.title: Structure and its end: Wolfe and Veracini read together
strands.focus: Two emphases within one formula, not a documented exchange between opponents. Wolfe's structure is 'a continuity through time' that 'does not stop' with frontier homicide and 'has not been subject to election results' (2006). Veracini accepts the 'frequently quoted passage' and adds that 'the structure persistently pursues a specific end point' and 'extinguishes itself', so that settler colonialism 'covers its tracks' (2011): the end point is the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, which Veracini distinguishes from decolonisation. The History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) records the two authors co-cited by 3.0% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, a readership pairing that does not itself establish a dispute. Englert reads both as drawing 'a sharp analytical separation' between eliminatory settler and exploitative franchise colonies and finds the separation does not fit Africa or South America (2020); Macoun and Strakosch find in the structure a 'colonial fatalism' and recall the label 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world' (2013): these readings establish different emphases placed on the same structure. Veracini's obituary records Wolfe as 'still a Marxist' of 'the young Marx' for whom 'things are not things in themselves but relationships' (2016).
strands.works: Wolfe, "Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native" (2006); Veracini, "Introducing settler colonial studies" (2011) and "Patrick Wolfe (1949–2016)" (2016); Macoun and Strakosch, "The Ethical Demands of Settler Colonial Theory" (2013); Englert, "Settlers, Workers, and the Logic of Accumulation by Dispossession" (2020).

strands.title: Canadian history beside and under the frame, 2009–2020
strands.focus: Works that Canadian PhDs read with Wolfe and Veracini, few of which adopt his vocabulary. Treaty history (Miller 2009, a distinctive riser among Canadian PhDs inside the Indigenous family in the 2026-10-23 release), racialisation and law in British Columbia's 'contact zone' (Mawani 2009), settler self-examination after residential schools (Regan 2010; Battell Lowman and Barker 2015: 'Canada and Settler Colonialism', 'It's Always All About the Land'), starvation policy (Daschuk 2013), Indigenous women's work 'in modern Native ways' (McCallum 2014), the TRC's finding that Canada's policy aimed 'to eliminate Aboriginal governments … and … cause Aboriginal peoples to cease to exist as distinct … entities' and 'can best be described as "cultural genocide"' (2015), imperial family and archive (Perry 2015), women homesteaders in 'the spadework of British colonialism' who 'took part in dispossessing Indigenous people' (Carter 2016), the settler-colonial city (Hugill 2017), the settler order in working-class history (Burrill 2019), Japanese Canadian dispossession (Stanger-Ross 2020), and Harris's reflections (2020). Veracini's own history says the Canadian historiography was 'late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis' (2013). Publisher descriptions, not the books, are read; none of Miller, Daschuk, McCallum, Perry 2015, Carter 2016 or Stanger-Ross uses the phrase on its page.

(2017); Burrill, "The Settler Order Framework" (2019); Stanger-Ross, ed., Landscapes of Injustice (2020); Harris, A Bounded Land (2020).

strands.title: A field's institutions: journal, associations, memorials
strands.focus: NAISA founded 2008 after an ASA panel of 2002 asked whether American Studies could be 'an intellectual home' for Native studies (Kauanui). Settler Colonial Studies founded 2011 'in an open access format (entirely run on volunteer labour)' and moved to Taylor & Francis 'within two years' (Snelgrove et al.; Edmonds and Carey 2013). Wolfe edited paired issues of the journal and of AICRJ (2013) and answered the binary charge with The Settler Complex (2016). ASA 2015: Goldstein's reappraisal and Warrior's count of panels. Wolfe's death (18 February 2016) brought obituaries from the journal (Veracini), AICRJ (Goeman), Aboriginal History (Birch) and an American Quarterly forum (2017); a Festschrift followed (Race, Place, Trace, 2022).
strands.works: Kauanui (2016); Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014); Edmonds and Carey, "A New Beginning for Settler Colonial Studies" (2013); Wolfe, ed., "Recuperating Binarism" (2013) and The Settler Complex (2016); Veracini (2016); Goeman (2016); Birch (2016); American Quarterly 69:2 (2017); Slyomovics and Veracini, eds., Race, Place, Trace (2022).
